observed_mechanics: 0x00c471c0 PUSH ECX pushes the incoming receiver into the slot that will later hold the argument for the +0x198 call, and 0x00c471ec overwrites that slot with the computed byte. This is a compiler slot-reuse artefact, not a second live variable, and it is why both exits need the ADD ESP,0x4.
0x00c471c6/0x00c471cc dispatch receiver vtable slot +0xf8 with no stack argument and read only AL afterwards (0x00c471ce TEST AL,AL), so the predicate is a byte.
0x00c471d0 JNZ 0x00c471e2 is the short-circuit: when slot +0xf8 already answers true, slot +0xfc is never consulted. 0x00c471d2 is only reached on the false path.
0x00c471d4/0x00c471da/0x00c471dc dispatch receiver vtable slot +0xfc with ECX reloaded to the receiver and no stack argument.
0x00c471e0 JZ 0x00c471e4 leaves AL at 0 when both predicates are false, so AL at 0x00c471e4 is exactly (slot_f8 OR slot_fc).
0x00c471e2 MOV AL,0x1 is the only writer of the predicate and it writes the whole low byte, never a dword, so the value is 0 or 1 with no undefined upper bits.
0x00c471e4/0x00c471ea/0x00c471f0 read the dword at +0x130, shift it right by one and test bit 0 of CL, i.e. bit 1 of the original dword.

0x00c471f3 JZ 0x00c47215 sends a clear bit 1 straight to the +0x198 exit; 0x00c471f5/0x00c471f7 JNZ 0x00c47215 does the same when the predicate is already set. Only bit 1 set AND predicate 0 falls through to 0x00c471f9.

0x00c471f9/0x00c471fb/0x00c47203 dispatch receiver vtable slot +0x19c with ECX = receiver and NO stack argument, even though the argument slot still holds the pushed receiver; the pushed word is never passed.
0x00c471c0 is 4 bytes before 0x00c471c4 and the two are unrelated, so there is no other receiver read in the function.
0x00c47217 reloads the predicate from the argument slot and 0x00c47221 pushes it, so slot +0x198 receives exactly one byte.

0x00c47205 and 0x00c47226 call 0x01046fc0, whose live body is `MOV EAX,[0x016e00d4]` with a lazy-create tail and a bare RET: it consumes nothing from the stack and returns the Simulator service singleton.

0x00c4720a/0x00c4722b move that singleton into ECX, and 0x00c47210/0x00c47231 JMP 0x01048ce0, so the flush call is a tail transfer from both exits and 0x01048ce0 is a thiscall void method on the service.

0x01048ce0's own body (read live) is: CALL 0x01021080; if the result is zero return; otherwise loop i=0..6 calling 0x01048c10(i) and then JMP 0x01047000. So the flush is guarded and drives seven per-index state transitions.

0x01048c10 (read live) validates its index against 0..7, reads the counter at this+4+index*4, and only acts when that counter equals 1, transitioning it to 0 or 3 depending on the index and dispatching to 0x01044a10, 0x01044df0, 0x01045c30 or 0x01048aa0.
0x00c471c0 appears nowhere in .rdata or .data as a dword (vtable scan total=0), so it is a non-virtual member and its class is not vtable-proven.

semantic_contract: Given a mission-like receiver, this function decides between two terminal actions and then flushes the Simulator. 1. It computes a single byte-valued predicate: predicate = vslot_0xf8() OR vslot_0xf8-false-then-vslot_0xfc(), short-circuited so that a true +0xf8 answer suppresses the +0xfc call entirely (0x00c471c4-0x00c471e2). The predicate is written only as AL, so it is exactly 0 or 1. 2. It reads the flag dword at +0x130 and tests bit 1 of it (0x00c471e4, 0x00c471ea, 0x00c471f0). 3. If and only if bit 1 is set AND the predicate is 0, it calls vslot_0x19c() with no argument (0x00c471f9-0x00c47203). In every other case - bit 1 clear, or the predicate already 1 - it calls vslot_0x198(predicate) with the predicate byte as its single argument (0x00c47215-0x00c47224). The +0x19c slot is never passed the argument that the function pushed at entry. 4. Both paths then obtain the Simulator service through 0x01046fc0 and tail-transfer to 0x01048ce0 on that service, which performs the guarded seven-step flush and then tail-transfers again (0x00c47205-0x00c47210 and 0x00c47226-0x00c47231). Invariants: exactly one of the two terminal slots is called on every invocation and never both; the flush runs exactly once per invocation on both paths; the function writes nothing in the receiver; its own single pushed word is removed on both exits, so the caller's stack is unchanged on return; and there is no RET instruction, so control never comes back.
classification_rationale: The complete body, the ABI including the unusual argument-slot reuse, the single field offset, the bit test, all four virtual slot numbers with their arities and result use, and both direct callees were read from the disassembly, and five callers were disassembled in full. It is not STRONG_SEMANTIC because: (a) OWNING CLASS - non-virtual with zero vtable hits, so cMission is a layout-and-slot-offset candidate; the four slot numbers and the +0x130 bit-1 agreement with cMission.h are strong but not vtable-proven, and the header's own names for slots +0x198 and +0x19c are unnamed reverse-engineered placeholders; (b) the concrete overrides behind all four slots are unresolved, so what 'fulfilled', 'failed', the +0x19c action and the +0x198 action actually DO is not established; (c) the domain meaning of the seven counters the terminal flush walks, and of the guard 0x01021080, is not established.
semantic_findings: The function is the last step of every mission SetState override in the binary and of at least one further mission method (0x00c47240). It is always reached by a tail JMP, so no caller ever inspects a result - it is a pure side-effect step.

Its own argument slot is reused: PUSH ECX at entry parks the receiver where the outgoing argument belongs, and 0x00c471ec overwrites it with the predicate. That is why both exits need ADD ESP,0x4 and why the +0x19c call, which needs no argument, simply ignores the parked word.
The two terminal slots are mutually exclusive by construction, so the function is a two-way selector rather than a sequence.

The +0x19c exit requires BOTH conditions, which makes it the rarer path: a caller can only reach it when the mission has accomplished nothing and the hide flag is set. The +0x198 exit is the fall-through and receives the predicate either way.
The predicate is a byte, not a dword: only AL is ever written, so there is no undefined-bits hazard for the callee even though the argument is pushed as a full word.
The Simulator flush is unconditional once the selector has run, and the selector runs unconditionally, so this function always ends in a flush regardless of which slot it chose.

0x01048c10, reached only through this function's tail, validates its index against 0..7 and acts only when the per-index counter equals 1, transitioning it to 0 or 3. That is a seven-slot state machine, and this function is one of its drivers.
unresolved_questions: Which class owns this function? It is non-virtual and appears in no vtable, so cMission stays a candidate. The callers are SetState overrides of several different derived mission types, so the receiver's concrete class varies per call site.

What do the four dispatched virtuals do? Slot +0xf8 and +0xfc are boolean predicates, +0x19c is a no-argument action and +0x198 takes that one boolean. cMission.h places HasBeenFulfilled, HasFailed, func19Ch and func198h at exactly those offsets with exactly those arities, but no vtable was found to confirm it and two of the four header names are placeholders.

What does the bit-1-of-+0x130 test mean in game terms? cMission.h names bit 1 kMissionFlagHideStarName, which would make the +0x19c exit a 'stop hiding the star name' action, but the SDK flag comments are themselves reverse-engineered and partly speculative.

What are the seven counters the terminal flush walks, and what does 0x01021080 guard? The flush body is known; the domain is not. The flush is skipped entirely when 0x01021080 returns zero, so on some runs this function's last action would be nothing at all.

Is the flush a no-op when the two virtuals did nothing? Both terminal slots have their results discarded, so if they are pure state changes with no dirty flag, the flush would be redundant - unresolvable statically.

Why does 0x00c47240 reach this function through a different path (after writing +0x100) while the SetState family reaches it right after 0x00c472e0? Both are consistent with 'last step of a refresh', but the trigger conditions differ and the reason is not established.
runtime_gates: No original-process trace exists for 0x00c471c0; every claim is static.
A runtime trace would be needed to see which of the two terminal slots is actually taken for a real mission transition, and to observe the seven counters the flush touches.
Naming the four overrides requires a receiver whose vtable base is known at run time.
